text: Deliver as many orders as possible across the town within the times we promised customers. The promised times (from order to pickup, and from pickup to delivery) may be revised if that is better than keeping promises we cannot keep. A change that is worse for customers needs a reason, given after measuring its effect on them.

title: On-time count as primary, with SLA-independent customer-impact monitors
reason: Recommended. This is the direct reading of 'as many orders as possible within the promised times'. The wait-time monitors give the human the measured customer effect that the KPI requires before accepting any change that is worse for customers, such as a looser SLA. No guard values are set because the KPI gives no levels.

title: On-time count as primary, monitoring only SLA-relative outcomes
reason: A literal reading that judges everything against the current promises. It is simpler, but every metric here moves when the SLA is redefined. An SLA loosening would look like a pure improvement, with no measurement of how much longer customers actually wait.

title: Actual customer wait as primary, on-time count monitored
reason: Robust against SLA gaming, but it shifts the main objective away from the KPI's stated goal of counting on-time deliveries. Use it only if the human considers actual speed to be the true intent.

reason: The KPI asks to maximize the number of orders delivered within the promised pickup and delivery times across the whole town, so the primary metric is on_time_deliveries. The promised times (DELIVERY_SLA) may be revised, but 'on time' is defined by the SLA itself. Loosening the SLA can raise on_time_deliveries without customers getting their orders any sooner. To measure the effect on customers, SLA-independent metrics are needed: the order-to-delivery wait times (p95_wait_s, max_wait_s) and unfinished orders. The KPI states no numeric levels, so no targets or guard values are set.

question: Which measure to use for the KPI from period 1
reason: The KPI asks to deliver as many orders as possible within the promised times, so on_time_deliveries is the primary goal. The KPI also allows revising the promised times, and it requires that a change worse for customers be justified by its measured effect on them. Option 2 judges everything against the SLA, so a looser SLA would look like a pure gain. That makes the required customer-impact measurement impossible. Option 3 moves the main objective away from the stated goal. Option 1 keeps the stated goal and adds SLA-independent monitors (p95_wait_s, max_wait_s, unfinished). These are the measurements needed before accepting any contract change. For now, 'worse for customers' means any increase in p95_wait_s, max_wait_s or unfinished. No numeric guard values are set because the KPI gives no levels. Fairness between companies is not part of the KPI as written.

reason: Neither option's main-goal gain is robust: both improve on-time on only 1 of 5 seeds, which is weaker evidence than the 2/5 you rejected in D2. Option 1 would also override B and C and push C's utility from 45.4 to 28.2 after C already lost in D1, while road violations rise by about 44%. Option 2 has no measured harm to customers and improves the customer monitors, but its mean gain likely comes from a single seed. question: Should we adopt block_k 3 → 2 (rejected by B and C), adopt hold_limit 60s → 70s (on-time gain seen on only 1 of 5 seeds), or keep the current rules (v2)?
reason: Under the K1 reading the main goal is on_time_deliveries, with p95_wait_s, max_wait_s and unfinished as customer monitors. Neither option's gain is robust. Option 1 raises on-time from 220.6 to 222.8 (+2.2), but only 1/5 seeds improved. Option 2 raises it from 220.6 to 222.6 (+2.0), also with only 1/5 seeds improved. In D2 I treated 2/5 seeds as too weak to act on, and I will not lower that bar now. Option 1 also overrides B and C (A ○, B ×, C ×). Its measured costs are large: B's utility falls from 73.6 to 55.0, C's from 45.4 to 28.2, and road violations rise from 23.4 to 33.6. Its customer gains are real (p95_wait_s 98.4 → 76.4, max_wait_s 146 → 128). Still, they do not justify overriding a majority vote when the main-goal gain shows on only one seed. Option 2 passed the vote and has no measured harm to customers. However, its mean gain likely comes from a single seed, and blocked s rises from 1322 to 1429. It should be measured again under next period's demand rather than adopted now. The current rules already deliver 220.6 on time, with 2.2 late, 0.0 unfinished and a lowest on-time rate of 0.98. This follows the LLM's recommendation. The vote passed option 2 only, and I decline it on the evidence. This decision also settles two open asks. K1.d.f2: no hard p95_wait_s or max_wait_s guard yet. The baselines have moved between periods (p95_wait_s 85.0 after D1, 116.4 in period 2, 98.4 now), and the KPI gives no level, so a fixed limit would be arbitrary. Any increase still counts as worse for customers, as set in K1. D1.f2: fairness stays outside the main KPI reading, as written. It remains the tie-breaker when the KPI gain is not robust, as in D2. C's utility under the current rules is 45.4, up from 19.2 after D1. Rejecting option 1 avoids a second large loss for C.
assumptions: The 5 seeds are representative of demand variation in busy periods.
The measured utilities reflect company interests accurately under fixed policies.
Keeping v2 carries no hidden deterioration beyond what the current-rules row shows.
unknowns: Whether option 2's gain holds on more seeds or under next period's demand.
How much of each option's mean gain comes from a single seed.
Whether option 1's extra road violations carry safety or third-party costs.
Why B voted against option 2 despite a small utility drop.
Next period's demand level.

title: hold_limit 60s → 70s (re-measure under period 4 demand)
reason: This carries out D3.f2. In period 3 the change raised mean on-time by 2.0, but on only 1/5 seeds, and blocked_s rose. Period 4 has heavier demand with a rush and 17 release overstays, so it tests whether a longer hold limit helps on more seeds. The change should cut deadline:release violations and B's and C's penalties, so B and C should vote yes. The risk is longer parking at node 8, which could raise blocked_s and A's 3 late pickups, so A may vote no and the main-goal gain may again be small or absent.
assumptions: Most of the 17 deadline:release violations are holds just over 60 s that would end within 70 s.
The simulator and seeds match those used for the period-3 measurement, so the seed count is comparable.
unknowns: Whether longer holds at node 8 add enough blocking to cause more of A's pickups to be late.
Whether any on-time gain shows on at least 2-3 of 5 seeds, the bar the human set in D2 and D3.
